Image size & uploads / FIELD GUIDE

How to compress an image to 100 KB or 200 KB for an online form

A form asks for a smaller photo. Here is how to meet the limit while keeping the face, text and edges clear.

By Manglo Editorial7 November 20267 min read
THE MANGLO PLAYBOOK / ORIGINAL GUIDE

“Image must be under 100 KB” is a familiar kind of upload error. A larger photo is not necessarily a better form photo, and an extremely compressed photo might be rejected for being unreadable. The goal is to satisfy the specific form's rules while keeping identifying details clear. A 100 KB target is not the same thing as a 100-pixel image.

1. Read the upload requirements first

Find four separate details on the form: accepted file type (usually stated as JPG/JPEG or PNG), maximum file size, pixel dimensions or aspect ratio, and any background or photo-content rules. Some portals also specify a minimum file size. Do not assume that the requirements of one exam, application, school or employer are the requirements of another. Check the live portal before editing.

Example, not an official form requirement

Imagine a portal accepts JPG images up to 200 KB and requires the subject to be clearly visible. Your objective is a JPG file at or below 200 KB that preserves adequate detail—not simply the smallest file possible.

2. Begin with a clear original image

Choose an in-focus photo with a well-lit subject. Keep a separate original, because shrinking and re-exporting the same already-compressed copy can cause additional quality loss. If the original is a PNG screenshot or photograph and the form accepts JPG, a JPG export may produce a smaller file. But JPG removes transparency, so it is not right for every graphic.

3. Reduce size in the right order

  1. Crop only if the form allows it. Remove needless empty space without cutting off required content.
  2. Resize to the required pixels. If the form specifies width and height, prioritize that requirement; do not invent a standard size.
  3. Choose an accepted format. JPG often suits photos, while PNG can be better for sharp text or graphics if allowed.
  4. Compress gradually. Try a moderate-quality output first and compare the result before pushing quality lower.

Manglo's target-size tool lets you upload a JPG, PNG or WebP image and request a limit such as 100 KB or 200 KB. Processing happens in your browser. The tool can adjust quality or dimensions as needed, but very detailed images might not reach an extremely low limit at acceptable quality.

4. Check the actual downloaded file

Open the exported file and verify its size in your device's file information. Also confirm its true format; renaming .png to .jpg does not convert it. Zoom in to check faces, lettering, signatures, borders or any element the application requires. Look at the complete photo again, then try the upload. If the portal still rejects it, read the exact error rather than repeatedly compressing.

Why a 100 KB export may still be rejected

What the form saysWhat to check next
File too largeInspect the downloaded file's actual KB/MB size.
Invalid file typeExport in the accepted format, not just a renamed extension.
Incorrect dimensionsCheck width × height in pixels and required orientation.
Photo unclearStart with a sharper original or use less compression.

A simple quality rule

Never sacrifice important details just to achieve a particular byte count. If the requirement cannot be met without severe blur, review the portal's precise specifications, start with a better source, and contact the form operator when necessary. The photo resizing guide explains how to control dimensions without distortion.

Technical reference: MDN image format guide.
